title: Can You Read Spanish? Latin? Catalan? The Library of Congress Needs Your Help
content:
Today’s post is from Lauren Algee, a Senior Digital Collections Specialist & By the People community manager at the Library of Congress. 

What can you learn about the history of Spain from a 500-year-old will?  How about a court ruling from the 1700s? These are the questions behind the transcription campaign for the Law Library of Congress’s Spanish Legal Documents collection. 

In 1941, the Library of Congress purchased the materials, as “a collection of covenants of judicial contests between people, noble men and civil and religious institutions in Spain – Reales Cédulas –Pragmáticas Reales of the XVIIth and XVIIIth centuries.” The collection then remained in the Law Library for over 40 years before funds were made available to organize, index, and photograph the documents for microfilm and make them available for public use. The collection was eventually digitized and published online, but aside from English language titles and short descriptions, the Law Library staff still have limited knowledge about the texts or the topics, individuals, and significant historical moments documented within the collection.

title: AI Sandbox Series: A Secure Environment to Explore Artificial Intelligence at the Library
content:
This post is the first in a series about the Library of Congress Artificial Intelligence (AI) Sandbox for staff. It provides an introduction to the initiative’s goals and an overview of the types of experiments conducted so far. Future posts will feature details about experiments in text recognition and searchability, metadata and bibliographic record enhancement, and more.

As the steward of over 200 petabytes of data including manuscripts, maps, books, images, artwork, audiovisual recordings, web archives, legislative data, research reports, and copyright records, the Library of Congress has spent decades building infrastructure and services to preserve and provide access to digital materials. The predictive and generative capabilities of artificial intelligence technologies offer enticing possibilities for maintaining, delivering, and analyzing some of the nation’s most influential research and treasured cultural and historical artifacts. Yet the use of these technologies requires extensive evaluation and monitoring before implementation.
